definition: Concurrent MetateM is a multi-agent language in which each agent is programmed using a set of (augmented) temporal logic specifications of the behaviour it should exhibit.
details: These specifications are executed directly to generate the behaviour of the agent. As a result, there is no risk of invalidating the logic as with systems where logical specification must first be translated to a lower-level implementation. MetateM is motivated by the separated normal form, where any formula in linear temporal logic can be rewritten as finitely many formulas of the form "past implies future". Execution proceeds by a process of continually matching rules against a history, and firing those rules when antecedents are satisfied. Any instantiated future-time consequents become commitments which must subsequently be satisfied, iteratively generating a model for the formula made up of the program rules.

explainer.lead: Concurrent MetateM is a language for programming multiple agents directly with temporal-logic rules about how they should behave. Because those rules are executed rather than translated into a separate implementation, the running behaviour stays tied to its logical specification.

tiers.eli5: Imagine giving each robot a set of rules such as, “If someone asked for a parcel, make sure it is eventually delivered.” The robot checks what has already happened, follows the matching rules, and remembers the promises it still has to keep. Several robots can each run their own rules at the same time.
tiers.practitioner: An engineer specifies each agent’s behaviour as augmented temporal-logic rules and lets the interpreter execute them directly. At each step, rule antecedents are matched against the execution history, while instantiated future consequents become outstanding commitments. The main implementation concern is therefore the ongoing satisfaction of those commitments, not maintaining a separate lower-level translation of the specification.
tiers.paperLevel: Each agent is a set of augmented temporal-logic specifications, motivated by separated normal form: any linear-temporal-logic formula can be rewritten as finitely many rules of the form past implies future. Execution repeatedly matches antecedents against the history, fires satisfied rules, and treats instantiated future consequents as commitments. Iteratively satisfying these commitments constructs a model for the formula formed by the program rules.

explainer.example: Suppose a delivery agent has a rule meaning, “If a delivery request occurred, eventually complete that delivery.” Once the request appears in its history, the rule fires and creates a commitment to complete the delivery; completing it satisfies that commitment. In Concurrent MetateM, other agents can execute their own specifications alongside it.

usedIn.name: Multi-agent systems
usedIn.detail: Each agent is programmed with its own temporal-logic specifications, and the agents execute concurrently.

usedIn.name: Executable agent specification
usedIn.detail: Logical behavioural rules serve directly as the agent program rather than as input to a separate implementation step.

explainer.intuition: Instead of writing a logical description and then separately coding an agent to match it, you make the description itself the program. Execution is a continuing cycle of recognizing what the past requires and fulfilling the resulting obligations about the future.
howItWorks: Write each agent’s behaviour as temporal-logic rules.
Keep a history of what has happened during execution.
Fire rules whose past-time antecedents match that history.
Turn their future-time consequents into commitments.
Satisfy commitments and repeat, generating behaviour over time.
explainer.whyItMatters: Direct execution removes the translation step in which a lower-level implementation could drift away from its logical specification. It also gives agent behaviour a clear execution model based on histories, rules, and commitments.
misconceptions: It is not a compiler that first turns temporal logic into a separate lower-level agent program.
Firing a rule does not necessarily finish its work: a future-time consequent can remain as a commitment to satisfy later.

diagram.caption: An agent repeatedly matches rules against its history, creates future commitments, and extends that history by satisfying them.
